paper.title: Evaluation of exposure-specific risks from two independent samples: a simulation study
paper.citation: Reichmann WM, Gagnon D, Horsburgh CR, Losina E. Evaluation of exposure-specific risks from two independent samples: a simulation study. BMC Medical Research Methodology 11:1 (2011)

simulation.what: The 'assumed population ESR' is RR x P(D|not E) unrounded (0.135 for the label .14), not the rounded label of the tables
simulation.sensitivity: The rounded label leaves {s1_label_within} of 112 cells of Table S1 and {s2_label_within} of S2 within tolerance (RMS z {s1_label_rms} and {s2_label_rms} against {s1_rms} and {s2_rms}); the population's realized ESR gives the same as RR x P(D|not E) (RMS z {s1_realized_rms} and {s2_realized_rms}). comparison.json, hypotheses.

simulation.what: When sample 2 has no cases among its exposed (or its unexposed), the log interval is (0, infinity): it covers, and it has no finite length, so it is left out of the expected length. The paper does not say.
simulation.sensitivity: Leaving those intervals out of the coverage instead (missing) gives Table S5 RMS z {s5_missing_rms} against {s5_rms} and puts the paper 1.5 to 3 points above us in Scenario 1 at N2 = 1000, in two runs; counting them as not covering leaves {s5_notcov_within} of 112 S5 cells within (RMS z {s5_notcov_rms}); adding 0.5 to the cells leaves {s7_half_within} of 112 S7 cells within (RMS z {s7_half_rms}). Only Scenario 1 at N2 = 1000 and the 250/250 runs have many such pairs (up to 39%).

simulation.what: One population of 10 million per setting, by Bernoulli draws of exposure and disease; both samples drawn from it without replacement, independently of each other; 1,000 pairs per setting; our own seeds
simulation.sensitivity: Exact cell proportions instead of draws change nothing (Tables S1, S2, S5, S7 112 of 112 each, exact_population in comparison.json). The seeds are ours: two runs of ours differ by more than the tolerance in {own_miss} of {own_cells} cells.

simulation.what: Comparison tolerance: half a printed unit plus 3 x sqrt(2) Monte Carlo standard errors of one 1,000-pair estimate, fixed before the comparison
simulation.sensitivity: With it two runs of our own design agree in {own_within} of {own_cells} cells ({own_pct}%). Wrong inputs (scenario or N1/N2 swapped) fall outside in {ctrl_out_min}% to {ctrl_out_max}% of the cells of Tables S1, S3, S5, S6 and S7; in Tables S2 and S4, where the true bias is 0 everywhere, a wrong input is almost as good as a right one.

figures.what: Bar heights read off the PMC figure JPEGs (600 x 464 px): y from the eleven tick labels, each bar's top where its column profile crosses half-way to its border's darkest pixel
figures.sensitivity: Tick fits within 0.00011 (0.15 px); one pixel is 0.00075, and is added to every bar's tolerance. Moving every bar by one pixel changes no verdict (each misses by 4 px or more, or passes by more than 1 px).

figures.what: The empirical CI in the figures is that of ESR_R (the caption says 'the direct estimator')
figures.sensitivity: The empirical CI of ESR_S is 2 to 189 px longer than the published bars and misses 9 of the 12 at the bars' tolerance; it is scored as a near-miss control.

eq10.summary: The paper's log CI of ESR_R behaves as if the first term of eq. 10, the variance of ln P1(D|not E), had been left out of the simulation (or computed as p(1-p)/n1, the variance of the proportion rather than of its log, which is close to 0). With eq. 10 as printed, our intervals cover more often, most of all at N1/N2 1000/5000 where that term is largest; without it, {s6_nofirst_within} of {s6_cells} cells of Table S6 (against {s6_within} with it) and {bars_nofirst_within} of {bars} bars of Figs 1-4 come back. The case study (Table 5) used eq. 10 as printed. The SAS code is lost, so this is read from the results.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The first term of eq. 10 is left out
hypotheses.test: Same samples, log CI of ESR_R without (1 - P1(D|not E)) / (n1 P1(D|not E)): Table S6 {s6_nofirst_within} of {s6_cells} (RMS z {s6_nofirst_rms}, against {s6_rms} as printed)

hypotheses.hypothesis: The first term is P1(D|not E)(1 - P1(D|not E))/n1, the variance of the proportion
hypotheses.test: Same samples with that term: Table S6 {s6_varnotlog_within} of {s6_cells}

hypotheses.hypothesis: n2 is used in place of n1 in the first term
hypotheses.test: Same samples with n2: Table S6 {s6_n2_within} of {s6_cells}

hypotheses.hypothesis: P1(D) is used in place of P1(D|not E) in the first term
hypotheses.test: Same samples with P1(D): Table S6 {s6_p1d_within} of {s6_cells}
Missing, not covering, or 0.5 added: Table S6 stays at {s6_zero_range} of {s6_cells}

hypotheses.hypothesis: The case study used the same shortened variance
hypotheses.test: Table 5: n1 solved from the binomial CI and Var(ln RR2) from the CI of ESR_S; the log CI of ESR_R predicted with and without the first term

chance.summary: Monte Carlo error: the paper's seeds are not given, and two runs of our own design differ by more than the tolerance in {own_miss} of {own_cells} cells ({own_miss_pct}%). Our second run, with another seed, puts each of these cells within tolerance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The cell is a chance miss of our run
hypotheses.test: The same design with another seed (replicate in comparison.json)

hypotheses.hypothesis: A systematic difference in the setting
hypotheses.test: No other cell of the same scenario and N1/N2 misses; the RMS z of the table is 0.97 to 1.22

case_rounding.summary: The case study's inputs are printed rounded (overall risk to 4 decimals, RR 1.91). From the printed inputs, ESR_S and ESR_R at ages 60-69 and 70-79 come out one unit low in the last digit (0.0166 against 0.0167, 0.0124 against 0.0125, 0.0281 against 0.0282, 0.0210 against 0.0211). An overall risk in [0.008719, 0.008750) and [0.014742, 0.014750), both of which round to the printed 0.0087 and 0.0147, gives every printed value.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Unrounded overall risks behind the printed ones
hypotheses.test: Scan P1(D) across its rounding interval for values giving both printed estimates

hypotheses.hypothesis: Another RR or P(obese) than printed
hypotheses.test: RR 1.91 and 0.371 give the printed 50-59 values exactly and every age with the scanned P1(D)

cause.summary: The paper ran in SAS 9.2 and released no code; none was found (issue #68 lists the search). The method was rebuilt from the text as esrisk and checked against the paper's tables and figures only.

items.label: Python package esrisk and its tutorial

page.lede: Reichmann and colleagues ran their simulation in SAS and published it in 2011 without the code. In November 2026 we rebuilt it from the paper and reran all 119 settings. Of {items} results, {agrees} agree, {partly} partly agree and {differs} differs. Every gap has a tested cause.
came_back: The bias of the two estimators
Tables S1 to S4 came back cell by cell within Monte Carlo error, one chance miss at most per table. ESR_S is off by up to 94% when exposure is common; ESR_R stays near 0.
The log interval of ESR_S (Table S5) and the binomial interval of ESR_R (Tables 4 and S7) came back the same way.
Every bar of Figs 1 to 4 for ESR_S, the binomial interval and the empirical interval came back within a few pixels.
The numbers given only in the text, Scenario 4 at 250/250, came back within Monte Carlo error.
Table 5 follows from its printed inputs to the last digit once their rounding is allowed for, and its interval of ESR_R follows from eq. 10 as printed.
esrisk, a Python package with the two estimators, the three intervals and the simulation, with a tutorial.
buried: The SAS programs. The paper names SAS 9.2 and released nothing; no copy was found.

The log interval of ESR_R in the simulation. Table S6 and the ESR_R bars of Figs 1 to 4 behave as if the first term of eq. 10 were left out; with it, as printed, our intervals cover more often. The case study used eq. 10 as printed.
The seeds. Each table carries Monte Carlo error; about one cell in a hundred misses by chance, as between two runs of our own.
page.matched_intro: What the paper does not say, and what we chose. Each choice was tested against the paper's tables.
matched: RR times the risk in the unexposed, unrounded (0.135, not the label .14). The rounded label misses many cells of Tables S1 and S2.
With no cases in one group of sample 2, the log interval is (0, infinity). Leaving those pairs out lowers coverage in Scenario 1; counting them as misses or adding 0.5 misses Tables S5 and S7.
10 million people per setting, both samples drawn without replacement. Fixed proportions instead of random draws change nothing.
Half a printed unit plus three combined Monte Carlo standard errors, fixed before the comparison.
page.closing: Reichmann and colleagues, 2011. The simulation came back in November 2026, from the paper alone.
page.items_caption: Each result of the paper, with the verdict computed from results.json and, for each one that is not exact, why.
page.tables_caption: Every cell of the supplement's seven tables and of Table 4. Tables 2 and 3 repeat cells of Tables S1, S2, S5 and S6 and are in the list below.
page.claims_line: The main claim holds: ESR_R removes the bias of ESR_S, and the binomial interval and the log interval of ESR_S behave as reported. The log interval of ESR_R does not, as printed: the paper's simulation left out the first term of eq. 10. The other claims that miss are chance, near the 95% line, or rounding.
